podcast.title: Band Formation and Longevity (1993-present)
podcast.body: Billy Talent formed in 1993, with the same four core members staying together since then. This long-standing lineup is considered an exception in the music industry, comparable to bands like Radiohead, U2 (since 1978), and ZZ Top (since 1969). The band members feel their identity is deeply intertwined with the band, having started at a young age, around 17.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: High School Formation (1993)
podcast.body: The band members first came together while they were all attending high school in Streetsville in 1993. "So we started in 1993. You guys are in high school? Yeah. We're all in high school together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's MS Diagnosis (1998)
podcast.body: Drummer Aaron Solowoniuk was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) in 1998 at the age of 24. His initial symptoms included buzzing legs, difficulty walking to his job at Chrysler, optic neuritis in his left eye (leading to vision loss), and confusion. He managed the disease for over a decade with medication, needle therapy, and a positive outlook.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's MS Diagnosis (1998)
podcast.body: Drummer Aaron Solowoniuk was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1998 at age 24, before the band's rise to fame, while working on an assembly line at a Chrysler factory. His initial symptoms included buzzing legs, difficulty walking, optic neuritis in his left eye resulting in vision loss, and general confusion. He managed the condition for over a decade with medication and a positive outlook. "What was 24? What were the symptoms? Buzzing legs from my hips down. I could barely walk to my job at Chrysler. I had an optic neuritis in my left eye, so I lost a lot of vision in my eye, and just being confused and trying to figure out what all that meant was really difficult."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: 1999-2003 - Life Distractions from Band
podcast.body: The period between 1999 and 2003 was challenging for the band, as members were in their early 20s, dealing with college, university, jobs, rent, and relationships, which pulled them away from the band. "It was like, there was that from 1999 to 2003, Ian and I went to a college in university, Ben went to college for a year. Aaron was, everything was just, it was just life happening in your early 20s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Years and Major Label Signing (2003)
podcast.body: The band toiled in obscurity for "eight, nine years" before their major label career began in the fall of 2003. Their break came when producer Gavin Brown and Mike McCarty saw them, leading to demo recordings and a publishing deal. Warner Canada then became interested due to their "first right of refusal" on the demos. The band experienced a "bidding war" involving Atlantic, Elektra, and Warner Brothers (US) over a month in August, with them being flown to New York for fancy dinners and performances. They were a "working class" band, all around 26 years old at the time, which made the experience surreal. "we went from toiling an obscurity for eight, nine years to then all of a sudden, literally within two weeks being flown back and forth to New York for a whole month, the whole month of August."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Evolution of Music Consumption (2003-2012)
podcast.body: The band has witnessed significant technological shifts in the music industry since the birth of the internet, including the rise of iPhones, streaming services, Facebook, MySpace, and Twitter by 2012. They acknowledge that record sales have never been their primary source of income, instead relying heavily on touring since their inception in 2003.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's MS Relapse and Album Absence (2016)
podcast.body: On January 15, 2016, Aaron announced on YouTube that he was experiencing an MS relapse, which had been slowing him down for six to seven months. The symptoms made it difficult to perform daily tasks and play drums. He decided to step away from recording drums for the "Afraid of Heights" album to focus on his health, as he was unsure how long his recovery would take. The band fully supported his decision and brought in Jordan Hastings as a fill-in drummer.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Band Support for Aaron Solowoniuk and FUMS (2016)
podcast.body: Billy Talent, their management, and their record label (Warner Music Canada) are 100% supportive of Aaron in his struggle with MS. They established a charity called FUMS (Fuck U MS) to raise money for MS research. At a music festival on May 29, 2016, a band member (Ben Kowalewicz) addressed the crowd, expressing the band's love, care, and commitment to Aaron, and thanking Jordan Hastings for filling in. The speaker referred to Aaron as "Mr. A. S. Lua," which appears to be a mis-transcription of his full name, Aaron Solowoniuk.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Relapse and Stepping Back from Recording (January 15, 2016)
podcast.body: In a YouTube message posted on January 15, 2016, Aaron Solowoniuk announced he was experiencing an MS relapse that had slowed him down over the past 6-7 months, making even simple tasks like climbing stairs daunting and drumming very tiring. Due to his health, he decided he couldn't play drums on the band's upcoming record and needed to focus on getting healthy. "On January 15th, 2016, Aaron posted a message on YouTube. Just wanted to let everybody know what is going on in Billy Talent World right now. The album is being recorded as we speak... Over the past six or seven months. I've been dealing with a relapse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: Unforeseen Rock am Ring Show (2016)
podcast.body: During a Rock am Ring Festival performance in 2016, bad weather and lightning strikes led to the evacuation of the grounds. The band was initially told they wouldn't play, with headliners Deftones and Red Hot Chili Peppers scheduled before them. Unexpectedly, the Red Hot Chili Peppers requested that Billy Talent go on after them, resulting in Billy Talent headlining. The next day, the festival was canceled due to weather. This was Jordan Hastings' third show with the band, with his first two having been in Russia.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: "Billy Talent 3" Label Rejection and Leak
podcast.body: The release of "Billy Talent 3" was marred by significant issues. The album was leaked online three months before its scheduled release. Two months prior, Warner US, who the band had signed with after leaving Atlantic, decided they no longer wanted to release it, with Tom Wally pulling the plug. This left them without a US label just before a worldwide release. They ultimately signed with Roadrunner Records last minute, but the leak and delayed US release "sabotaged the record," leading labels to "pull back on the whole release." "it got leaked and then two months before it was supposed to come out Warner US decided that they didn't want to release it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's Treatment and Recovery
podcast.body: After his relapse, Aaron decided to stop taking his MS medication for three months and explore alternative therapies, focusing on healthy eating and exercise. He expressed a goal to come back stronger, listening to his body more carefully, after having previously pushed himself too hard, to the point of walking with a cane. In 2017, he made a return to the stage, playing one song in Poland, his first performance in a year.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Aaron's Battle with MS
podcast.body: The band has collectively supported Aaron, the drummer, through his battle with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) "from day one." "we'll talk about Aaron's battle with MS something that has been a group effort from day one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Aaron's Dad - Chrysler Truck Access
podcast.body: Aaron Solowaniak's father, who worked for Chrysler, allowed the band to borrow large trucks to transport their stolen milk crates and plywood for their self-organized shows. "Like, Aaron's dad worked for Chrysler too. So we bore these large trucks and, and basically not steel, but borough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The Canadian band "Billy Talent" adopted their name from the character "Billy Talent," who was the guitarist in the 1996 film "Hardcore Logo." "It also featured a guitarist named Billy Talent and yes that's where the name came from."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Band Rebirth - Name Change, New Songs, New Rehearsal Space
podcast.body: Following a period of struggles and individual pursuits, the band experienced a "rebirth." This was catalyzed by Ian D'Sa bringing in new songs like "Try Honesty" and "Cut the Curtains," Ben Kowalewicz suggesting a band name change (from Pezz to Billy Talent), and acquiring a new rehearsal space. "And then Ben suggested we change the band name and everything just kind of came together all at once and it did feel like a rebirth and we got a new rehearsal space down the front and sure burn over here and we felt like a real band again and was up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Support and Charitable Work
podcast.body: Despite Aaron Solowoniuk's ongoing health challenges and reduced ability to play, Billy Talent continues to support him. The band also engages in numerous charitable initiatives with MS groups, demonstrating their commitment to raising awareness and funds for the disease. "It's been tough for Aaron and he hasn't been able to play with the band as much as he'd hoped but he's still with the guys and the guys are still supporting him, including with numerous charitable initiatives with MS groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: Best Territory in Canada
podcast.body: Despite international success, Canada remains Billy Talent's best territory, with hometown shows holding significant special meaning for the band.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Canadian Music Week - Critical Acclaim
podcast.body: The band received positive "report cards" at Canadian Music Week, scoring 93% in 1999 (making them a Top 10 act) and 94% in 2000. These strong reviews garnered attention from industry professionals. "So like we, so in 1999, we had a 93% report card. So we made it into their like top 10 thing. And then 2000, we made it again. We had a 94. And all of a sudden, all these industry people started paying attention to us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Canadian Rock Band of 21st Century
podcast.body: Billy Talent is described as one of the biggest Canadian rock bands to emerge in the 21st century. "And the result is an unvarnished history of one of the biggest Canadian rock bands to emerge in the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Challenges with US Labels
podcast.body: The band faced persistent difficulties with US labels and management. After the initial success of "Try Honesty," Atlantic Records decided not to release another single from their debut album, citing commitments to "bigger artists" and the approaching Christmas season. In 2004, Warner America, facing financial trouble due to fear of Napster and declining CD sales, dumped around 200 artists. The band was nearly dropped, but their second record's sales (around 60,000 units, exceeding the 50,000 threshold for dropping) saved them, though they "wanted to get dumped" due to lack of support. "And in the States, we released Tri-Honesty and it did quite well and then the label had a choice to release another single and they didn't. And that was kind of the beginning of our open battle with America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Collaborated with Weezer
podcast.body: Weezer had guest appearances and writing credits with Billy Talent. "Billy Talent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 2

podcast.title: Commitment to Artwork and Physical Sales
podcast.body: From day one, Billy Talent has prioritized creating great artwork to accompany their albums. For "Dead Silence," they worked with Kent Taylor, known for his band-related artwork and silk screen art. This focus is particularly relevant in markets like Germany, South Korea, and Japan, where physical music sales (vinyl, deluxe box packages) still account for a significant portion of the market (e.g., 67% in Germany).

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Creative Drive for Second Album
podcast.body: The band approached their second album with intense ambition, viewing it as their "big shot" where a "crappy second album" could end their career. This drive led them to make the songs "the best they can possibly be" and expand their sound, despite constantly being on the road for a year and a half to two years. "it's the wanting to outdo yourself and you know that your second album is that that's your big shot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Croatian Cultural Center Performance
podcast.body: Billy Talent and Alexis on Fire co-headlined a show at the Croatian Cultural Center in Vancouver, drawing a thousand people, which was described as one of the best nights of their lives. "Literally play the Croatian Cultural Center in Vancouver with Billy Talent to a thousand people and it'd be one of the best nights of our life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: DIY Stages - Milk Crates and Plywood
podcast.body: In their early days, when there were no official venues, the band would organize their own shows, constructing stages by "stealing" milk crates from behind grocery stores and drywall/plywood from local housing units under construction in Mississauga. "And then when we would have the show, we would put the milk cartons together and tape them up and steal drywall from local, like housing units and make our own stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Demoluca Rarity
podcast.body: Only about 100 copies of the "Demoluca" demo tape were made, making it a rare item that can now occasionally be found for sale on platforms like eBay. "There was only a hundred copies made. Well, look at this. From Demoluca, here's Pez, and Happy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Before They Were Famous

podcast.title: Early Canadian Tour
podcast.body: Billy Talent toured across Canada with Alexis on Fire and Death from Above around 2002-2003, during the period of Alexis on Fire's first record. This tour allowed both bands to see a country-wide audience of 500-600 capacity venues. "We went across Canada with death from above. And that was, yeah, that was where we got to see it every night, you know, because we had only played Southern Ontario really."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Early Career Venues
podcast.body: In their early days, Billy Talent performed in a wide variety of settings, including bars, clubs, Chinese food restaurants, and even house parties, emphasizing their roots and consistent dedication to live performance. They originate from Streetsville, Ontario.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Early Toronto Breaks
podcast.body: The band, as Pez, got their first significant break in downtown Toronto by giving their "Demoluca" tape to William New, who booked "Elvis Mondays" nights at the Old Elmucongo. A last-minute cancellation led to their first gig there, which opened doors to further bookings and connections with other Toronto bands. "Our first big break downtown was we gave this tape to a guy named William New, who had the oldest Mondays at the Old Elmucongo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Before They Were Famous

podcast.title: Evolution from Pez
podcast.body: Billy Talent initially went by the name Pez in the early 1990s, recording their first four-song demo, "Demoluca," in 1994. "That's Billy Talent from 1993, when they were still trading under the name Pez."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Before They Were Famous

podcast.title: Exploring Alternative MS Management
podcast.body: Aaron Solowoniuk decided to stop taking all prescribed drugs for three months, as newer medications had not worked and made him feel worse. He is now pursuing a regimen of healthy eating and exercise, hoping to manage his MS symptoms naturally, with a plan to explore newer therapies if this approach proves ineffective. "Right now I've stopped taking all of my... I'm three months into no drugs at all. I'm going the eating healthy and exercising route to see how that works because the drugs that I've been taking, the newer ones, haven't really worked for me and they kind of made me feel worse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: Featured in "In Their Own Words" Series
podcast.body: Billy Talent was featured in the "In Their Own Words" series, which gathers band members to share their personal histories. "Billy Talent, Matthew Good..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Jam Session - Unproductive to Productive
podcast.body: The band's initial jam session in July 1993 was unproductive, characterized by "noises and sucking." However, their second jam, which involved covering Neil Young's "Keep On Rockin' in the Free World," allowed them to complete a full song, giving them confidence. "I remember the first jam basically nothing productive happened. We just made noises and we sucked. And I remember us three being like, I wonder if this is going to work out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Ian's Parents' Basement - Milk Crate Storage
podcast.body: Ian D'Sa's parents' basement served as a storage location for the milk crates and plywood used for their DIY stages. At one point, there were approximately 500 milk crates stored there, causing the basement to reek of spoiled milk. "I remember one time there was like 500 milk crates in Ian's basement and his mom would come down and say, Ian, what are you doing with all these milk crates? Don't worry, mom, it's all good. Well, my parents' basement wreaked like, like, like, broad milk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Importance of Live Performance
podcast.body: The band has always prided itself on its live shows and touring. They believe that a live performance cannot be downloaded, requiring fans to buy a ticket and experience it in person. Their dynamic on stage has been a source of significant pride since their beginnings, from playing small venues to large festivals.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Influenced by Blink-182
podcast.body: Billy Talent is listed among the artists who draw influence from Blink-182, suggesting a connection in their musical approach or inspiration. "Some 41 good Charlotte simple-plan panic at the disco, followed boy, headly, billy talent, you would meet six, paramour, you know, you get the idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: International Fan Base in Europe
podcast.body: Billy Talent received funding and support, including from programs like Radio Star Maker, which enabled them to tour overseas. This strategic international touring resulted in the band developing a sizable fan base in Europe, particularly in Germany. "And that kind of help has done wonders for bands like Billy Talent when they wanted to or overseas. And that's resulted in a sizable fan base in Europe, especially in Germany."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Jen Hurst - Discovery and Support
podcast.body: Jen Hurst, who initially worked at a defunct label before becoming Junior A&R at Warner Music Canada, discovered Pezz at the 360 Club. She saw potential in the band and continued to support them, eventually making them a top priority for signing at Warner. "And Jen Hurst was working at this one label, which is now to funk, which I can't remember. And I remember talking to her and her and I got along really well. And I said, I'm in a band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Label Staff Turnover Impact
podcast.body: A significant challenge for the band in the US was the frequent turnover of label staff, where their "champions" (A&R reps who believed in them) were repeatedly fired. This left them working with new personnel who had no vested interest in the band, leading to a lack of sustained support and preventing them from reaching the "next level." This occurred "four times in the States." "all the people that we had met and all the people that were our quote unquote champions to like help us, they all got fired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Members Ages at Formation
podcast.body: At the time of their first jam session in July 1993, the band members were either 17 or 18 years old. "18. 17. 17. 18."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Multiple Warped Tour Appearances
podcast.body: Billy Talent has participated in the Warped Tour four times. "Billy Talant four times as a matter of fact."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 24 Years of the Warped Tour

podcast.title: No Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Since its formation in 1993, the core lineup of Ben Kowalewicz, Ian D'Sa, John Gallant, and Aaron Solowaniak has remained constant, aside from some temporary situations. "Never. No. Never. That's insane. Yeah. There's been some temporary things here and there, but this has been the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Pez - Rage Against The Machine Comparison
podcast.body: When Ben Kowalewicz left his radio job to pursue the band, his then-boss, Phil Evans, described the band as being "kind of like Rage Against The Machine." "Yeah, he's got this band that, you know, they're kind of like rage against the machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Production Involvement of Ian
podcast.body: During the recording of "Billy Talent 2" at The Warehouse at Brown Island Studio in Vancouver, Ian, the main songwriter, became more involved in the production process, recognizing his ability to contribute to that aspect of the music. "it's also where Ian became more involved in the production as well, because he's always been the main songwriter in the band. It's when Ian kind of first went, oh, I can kind of, I get this and I want to kind of dip this feet in the production waters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Seed Money from Nickelback Profits
podcast.body: Billy Talent's deal with Roadrunner Records in the US received "seed money" that indirectly originated from the profits generated by Nickelback's album sales. This illustrates how successful bands like Nickelback contribute to the broader music industry by funding new acts and ventures for other artists on the same label. "When Billy Talent had a deal with the roadrunner in the US, where do you think some of that seed money came from? Uh-huh. Nickelback record sales."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 10 Things That Really Annoy Me

podcast.title: Shared Rise to Prominence
podcast.body: Billy Talent and Alexis on Fire experienced a similar breakthrough around the same time, with both bands gaining opportunities and radio attention with songs like "Pulmonary Archery" and "Try Honesty." They shared a Canadian tour alongside Death from Above, playing larger venues and witnessing the demand for aggressive music across the country. "And I think when the, when Palm and I started getting played across Canada, it was the same time Billy Talent and Tri-Honesty started clicking and they started getting radio attention as well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Signing with Atlantic Records
podcast.body: The band ultimately signed an 80/20 split deal with Atlantic Records for the world and America, while Warner Canada retained rights for Canada. This decision was influenced by the legendary status of Atlantic, known for artists like Led Zeppelin. They even met Ahmet Ertegun, one of Atlantic's co-founders, in his office on the day of signing, where they saw Jimmy Page's bow from "The Song Remains the Same" on the wall. "And so we decided to go with Atlantic records, which was the originally in our guys that we had seen that came up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Songwriting Process
podcast.body: Ben and Ian collaborate on lyrics, which typically begin after the music is completed. For their first record, many songs were years in the making, while others, like "River Below," were written more quickly. Ian often uses "little recorders" and acoustic guitar to work on tunes while on the road. "Ian and I have always done it together you know so we would always wait till and still to this day when the music is done that's when the lyrics kind of would start."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Strong German Market
podcast.body: Germany is a country where Billy Talent performs exceptionally well, demonstrating a robust fanbase there, particularly evident at events like the Rock am Ring Festival.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Success in Europe (Germany and UK)
podcast.body: Despite US struggles, Billy Talent achieved significant success in Europe, particularly Germany and the UK. This was attributed to extensive touring in small clubs on their first album, opening for bands like The Beatsteaks, and strong label support that ensured radio and MTV play. They prioritized investing their time and energy in Europe, playing festivals there due to a strong "festival culture," rather than "half sold rooms" in the States. "we put in the time there. We played every small club in Germany on the first album and we got the right tours opening up for the one of the best punk bands there called the Beat Stakes. And it just took off organically."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Tom Wally's Unusual Meeting
podcast.body: When Warner Brothers President Tom Wally wanted to meet Billy Talent, he refused to leave his New Jersey beach house. The band was flown to New Jersey, played a "s***ly little session" in a rented airplane hanger with unfamiliar gear, while Wally sat looking at the floor, preoccupied with his house. After the performance, he still wanted to sign them but only allowed them to eat on his patio during a family birthday, providing fried chicken and beer. "Tom Wally had, he wanted to see us. He was the president of Warner Brothers. And he didn't want to leave his beach house in New Jersey to come to the city. So they took us to New Jersey, rented an airplane hanger. We played the s***ly little session in front of him."

podcast.title: Unique Guitar Playing Style
podcast.body: Ian, the band's guitarist, developed a unique, self-taught playing style that combines rhythm and lead parts due to being the sole guitarist. He achieves this by playing in drop D tuning, which allows him to play bar chords with one finger while doing leads with the others, describing it as "almost like piano playing." He was influenced by clean players like Andy Summers and Mark Knopfler, as well as Tom Morello and Kim Thayil, and consciously avoided traditional playing. His style is considered "the most unique in the world." "I ended up trying to do both when I became the sole guitar player in this band. And by doing that, I found like dropping to D, I could play, I could play bar chords with one finger and then do a bunch of leads with the other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Vocal Style Development
podcast.body: Ben, the vocalist, initially spent the first five years of the band trying to emulate other singers like Eddie Vedder, Scott Weiland, and Zack de la Rocha. He eventually realized he couldn't sound like them and developed his own distinctive style. This unique vocal approach, combined with Ian's guitar playing, helped the band stand out from other Canadian bands of the era like Moist, Treble Charger, and The Tea Party. "I, the first five years of being in a band, you know, I was trying to sound like other people, you know, I was trying to sound like Eddie Vetter. I was trying to sound like Scott Watt. I'm trying to sound like Zack Delroch. You know, like, I'm trying to do that. And then I realized I can't do that, you know, so I just kind of ended up being me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warner Music Deal - Jen Hurst's Role
podcast.body: Jen Hurst's belief in the band, her move to Warner Music Canada as Junior A&R, and the positive reviews from Chartattack led to Pezz being at the top of her list of indie bands to sign, ultimately leading to their record deal. "That was the TSN turning point in a lot of ways. And then she got the job at Warner and the ASTAS, as her, who her top favorite indie bands in the city were that she would consider signing. And we were on the top of her list."

xref.title: Stepping Back from Recording Drums (2016)
xref.body: On January 15, 2016, Aaron Solowoniuk announced via YouTube that he would temporarily step away from recording drums for Billy Talent's upcoming album due to an MS relapse. He explained that his symptoms were slowing him down, and he needed to focus on his health, expressing uncertainty about the duration of his recovery. "I'm not going to be able to play drums on this record. I just need to focus on my health while the record is being recorded."

xref.title: Career vs. Health Benefits Dilemma (Early 2000s)
xref.body: As Billy Talent gained traction, Aaron faced a choice between continuing his factory job at Chrysler, which offered good benefits covering his expensive MS drugs, and pursuing music with the band, which typically lacked such benefits. He ultimately chose the band, initially keeping his condition a secret. "Working at the Chrysler plant meant good benefits, benefits that covered the cost of the expensive drugs he needed. Meanwhile, rock bands tend not to have any benefits."

xref.title: Decision to Not Play on Latest Album
xref.body: Aaron made the difficult decision not to participate in recording Billy Talent's latest album approximately one month before they were scheduled to enter the studio, after 12 or 13 songs had already been written. At this point, he was using a cane and felt he was pushing himself too hard, acknowledging that his MS was finally slowing him down despite his long-held determination not to let it. "We had written 12 up 13 songs and we were one month away from going into the studio and I just said I can't do it."

xref.title: Impact on Music Industry Ecosystem
xref.body: Despite widespread criticism and "irrational global hatred," Nickelback is recognized as a vital component of the music industry's ecosystem. Their commercial success and high album sales meant they were a "hit band" that generated substantial profits. This revenue, particularly during their tenure with Roadrunner Records, was instrumental in subsidizing releases for numerous metal bands such as Opeth, Killswitch Engage, and Mastodon, and also provided crucial "seed money" for Billy Talent's entry into the US market. They exemplify the "rule of 30" in music, where a few highly successful acts financially support many others. "They are an important part of the music industry ecosystem."

xref.body: Blink-182 is considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century. Their style and career trajectory have left a significant mark on numerous artists across the genre, inspiring bands like Sum 41, Good Charlotte, Simple Plan, Panic! At The Disco, Fall Out Boy, Hedley, Billy Talent, You Me At Six, and Paramore. "Blink has to be considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century."

xref.title: Inspiration for Career Trajectory
xref.body: Pearl Jam is cited by Billy Talent as a source of inspiration due to their career path, which includes periods of "tremendous success" followed by albums where they "fell off a bit," only to later return with "big splash and great songs and sold out tours." This resilience resonated with Billy Talent, especially during the "weird time" surrounding their "Billy Talent 3" album. "not to reference Pearl Jam but you know a band like Pearl Jam they've had that you know I always look to them as a source of inspiration because they've had tremendous success and then they've had some records where they just kind of fell off a bit and then you know and then eight years later they're back with this big splash and great songs and sold out tours."

xref.title: Mellotron Usage

He later used this same Mellotron on Billy Talent's songs "Saint Veronica" and "White Sparrows" from the album "Billy Talent III," after the band expressed their admiration for its sound.

xref.title: Pop Music Shift
xref.body: The rise of Alexis on Fire and similar aggressive bands coincided with a shift in pop music in the mid-2000s. Fans who had grown up with pop acts like Backstreet Boys, N'Sync, Christina Aguilera, and Britney Spears from the mid-90s were aging and seeking music that expressed anger, fears, and frustrations, creating an opening for bands like Alexis on Fire and Billy Talent. "But during that time, we were seeing the end of the spike in pop music, you know, the back street boys and instincts and Christine Aguilar is in Britney Spears and that group of people who had been into pop since the middle 90s with spice girls and whatever, they were now getting older and they were getting angry and they were looking for something that spoke to that anger and their fears and their frustrations."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Lives
xref.body: Following the band's breakup, members pursued different paths: Dallas Green continued with City and Colour, George Pettit became a firefighter, Wade McNeil became a radio DJ, Jordan Hastings became a fill-in drummer for Billy Talent and played in other bands, and Chris Steele was last heard to have gone for a "truck on the Himalayas." "I mean, Dallas Green is off doing a city and color thing. Vocalist George Pettit became a firefighter. Wade McNeil is doing a bunch of stuff, including working as a radio DJ. Drummer Jordan Hastings is filling it with Billy Talbot and playing in some other bands. And I'm not even sure where bass player Chris Steele is."

xref.title: Touring Challenges
xref.body: The band experienced significant disparity in audience numbers during their early tours. For example, they played a successful show at the Croatian Cultural Center in Vancouver to a thousand people with Billy Talent, only to cross the border into Bellingham, Washington, and play for only the bar staff, with Dallas Green not even performing due to voice issues. Later, attempts to "hammer it" in America during the "Old Crows" era, including a "disastrous" Warped Tour and long unfulfilling American tours where only 40-60% of shows were good, became mentally exhausting. "We played for the bar staff. I don't even think I played the show. You didn't. I didn't. I took a T-shirt. Because your voice was bothering you."
